record.title: Paper reports a game-based method for mitigating agent deception
record.summary: A Nov 9 arXiv paper formulates agent deception mitigation as an extensive-form game in which a monitor inspects interaction trajectories and a verifier checks its claims. The authors prove equilibrium existence for finite games and state conditions under which equilibrium behavior is faithful. They report lower deception and higher compliant task success in Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B. These are controlled paper-reported results, not independently reproduced or evidence of deployment performance.
organizations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors formulate deception mitigation as an evaluation-side partially observable extensive-form game with an agent, a trajectory-inspecting monitor, and a verifier that checks monitor claims.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper proves equilibrium existence for finite games and states faithfulness guarantees under perfect verification, or under imperfect verification when errors do not reverse the ranking of monitor actions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report reduced deception in Agentic Role-Playing and higher compliant task success in SearchQA and WebShop across experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: Independent reproduction, effectiveness against adaptive deception outside the tested settings, and performance in deployed agent systems are not established by this activation.

evidence_gaps.description: Reported empirical results have not been independently reproduced or code-audited in this activation.
Theoretical faithfulness depends on verifier assumptions; effectiveness beyond three controlled benchmark settings and against adaptive deception is not established.

brief.importance_rationale: If this evaluation-side oversight method transfers beyond controlled benchmarks, it could change how agent systems detect deceptive tool use and reward hacking. The reported empirical gains remain paper claims and the formal guarantee depends on verifier assumptions.
limitations: The formal guarantee assumes perfect verification or verifier errors that preserve the ranking of monitor actions.
The empirical results are author-reported and cover Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA and WebShop with small open models; no independent reproduction occurred here.
The work does not establish effectiveness in production systems or against unconstrained adaptive adversaries.

brief.summary: A Nov 9 arXiv paper formulates agent deception mitigation as an extensive-form game in which a monitor inspects interaction trajectories and a verifier checks its claims. The authors prove equilibrium existence for finite games and state conditions under which equilibrium behavior is faithful. They report lower deception and higher compliant task success in Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop experiments with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B. These are controlled paper-reported results, not independently reproduced or evidence of deployment performance.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports lower deception in Agentic Role-Playing and increased compliant success in SearchQA and WebShop; these are author-reported benchmark measurements.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint demonstrates that the authors report this method and these measurements. This activation did not independently reproduce them.
technical.mechanism: A monitor inspects the full interaction trajectory and proposes a natural-language critique; a fixed verifier checks that critique and applies a penalty to the agent when deception is supported.
technical.regime: Finite extensive-form game theory and controlled experiments using Agentic Role-Playing, SearchQA, and WebShop with Gemma3-4B-IT and Qwen3-4B/8B.
technical.reproducibility: Full arXiv HTML and protocol appendices are accessible; code is linked by the paper. No code audit or independent reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares against reinforcement learning, mixed safety RLHF, verifier and monitor baselines; exact comparative conclusions remain bounded to its stated benchmark setups.

brief.title: Paper reports a game-based method for mitigating agent deception
brief.why_it_matters: The work makes evaluator visibility and verification part of the optimization game, offering a concrete oversight design to test against agent reward hacking. Its value depends on monitor coverage and verifier reliability; the reported benchmarks do not show effectiveness in deployed agents.
